sections.title: Hungry Nation: Food, Health, and Power in South Asia
sections.description:
Increased production of food has transformed not just human lives but also our planet. According to the UN report on the Right to Food, global food production is a major driver of environmental disasters, metabolic disorders, and undernutrition. Despite rising food stocks, a large portion of the world’s population faces recurring patterns of food insecurity, a situation that has only become worse following the COVID-19 pandemic. This course explores the origins and persistence of such contradictions within our contemporary food systems by exploring the
politics of food and hunger in South Asia, a region central to discussions of global hunger.
How, what, where, and with whom South Asians eat has cultivated notions of collective belonging and identity, shaped the politics of anti-colonial nationalism, and at the same time entrenched unequal relations of agricultural production and reinforced practices of social exclusion. Drawing from perspectives and approaches in history, anthropology, science and technology studies, global health, and critical food and environmental studies, we will learn to pose and craft answers to questions such as:
Are hunger and famine natural disasters, or are they shaped by intersections between society, science, and the state? Have scientific and technological interventions in food production and consumption disrupted practices of social exclusion or further reinforced them? What does it mean to patent seeds as technologies when they have been in use for centuries? Finally, can
changing our relationship with food transform our health, collective life, and the environment? To understand how experts, political and social elites, and ordinary people have differently confronted, understood, and addressed the problem of hunger, we will read political and social commentaries, policy and scientific debates, poetry and literature, and analyze popular audio-visual materials.
